'''Ken-Ichi Honma''' (born in November 10, 1946) is a Japanese [[Chronobiology|chronobiologist]] who researches the [[Biology|biological]] mechanisms underlying [[circadian rhythm]]s. After graduating from [[Hokkaido University]] School of Medicine, he practiced [[Clinical psychology|clinical psychiatry]] before beginning his research. His recent research efforts are centered around photic and non-photic [[Entrainment (chronobiology)|entrainment]], the structure of [[Circadian clock|circadian clocks]], and the [[ontogeny]] of circadian clocks. He often collaborates with his wife, [[Sato Honma]], on work involving the [[Suprachiasmatic nucleus|mammalian suprachiasmatic nucleus]] (SCN). 

He was born in [[Sapporo]], [[Hokkaido]], and currently lives with Sato Honma, his wife, in Japan, with their only daughter.<ref name=":6" />

Honma serves as the chairman of the Keiaikai Sapporo Hanazono Hospital, and is a [[professor emeritus]] at Hokkaido University.

== Education and career ==

In 1971, Honma received his [[Doctor of Medicine|Doctorate of Medicine]] and then his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D]]. in Medicine in 1977 from the Hokkaido University School of Medicine. He worked as an assistant professor at Hokkaido University until 1978, when he left to perform research at the [[Max Planck Society|Max-Planck Institute]] in [[Andechs]], [[Germany]], as a [[postdoctoral fellow]]. He first worked with Professor Wolfgang Wuttke in [[Göttingen]], then with [[Jürgen Aschoff]]. In 1983, Honma was promoted to [[associate professor]] and began working on experiments involving the human circadian clock in [[temporal isolation]]. In 1992, he became a full-time professor at the Hokkaido University School of Medicine.<ref name=":6">{{cite web | vauthors  = Honma KI | title = Curriculum Vitae | url = https://srbr.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/HonmaKI_CV.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Ken-ichi Honma — Intercontinental Academia |url=http://intercontinental-academia.ubias.net/nagoya/people/ken-ichi-honma |access-date=2024-05-07 |website=intercontinental-academia.ubias.net}}</ref>

Honma was the former vice-president of the Japanese Society of Sleep Research (2007–2021), the former council chair of the Japanese Society for Chronobiology (2005–2011).<ref name=":5" />

He is the vice-president of the Asian Society of Sleep Research (ASRS), the prior Editor-in-Chief of ''Sleep and Biological Rhythms,'' an English Journal of the Japanese Society of Sleep Research and the Asian Society of Sleep Research, and an associate member of the Science Council of Japan.<ref name=":5" /> Since 2016, Honma has also been a member of The Committee of ChronoHistory.<ref>{{cite web | title = ChronoHistory | access-date = April 20, 2021 | url = https://www.clocktool.org/clock-modules/chronohistory.html | archive-date = April 20, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210420230714/https://www.clocktool.org/clock-modules/chronohistory.html | url-status = dead }}</ref> Honma is the chairman of the Sapporo Symposium on Biological Rhythms (1995–present), which holds an international symposium centered around chronobiology biannually. He served as the head of a Japan-U.S. joint project on Biological Timing, where he was responsible for sending many Japanese scientists to the United States (1993–1995).<ref>{{cite web|title=Ken-ichi Honma — Intercontinental Academia|url=http://intercontinental-academia.ubias.net/nagoya/people/ken-ichi-honma|access-date=2021-05-05|website=intercontinental-academia.ubias.net}}</ref> While he was the president-elect of the Japanese Society of Chronobiology (2005 to 2010), he co-organized the biannual meetings of the European Biological Rhythms Society (EBRS) and held the first world congress of chronobiology in 2003 at Sapporo as the founding president of the World Federation for Societies of Chronobiology (2001–2011). He has tried to establish a forum among Chronobiologists in Asia as the council chief of the Asian Forum on Chronobiology (2015).<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|title=President Ken-ichi Honma's profile|url=https://aschoff-honma.wixsite.com/ahmf/pre|access-date=2021-05-05|website=ahmf|language=ja}}</ref>

===Awards and honors===
In 2020, Honma received the SRBR Director’s Award for mentoring.<ref>{{cite web | title = SRBR Director's Award for Mentoring | work = Burroughs Welcome Fund Excellence Awards | url = https://srbr.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Winners_For-Website.pdf | publisher = Society for Research on Biological Rhythms | date = 2020 }}</ref> The SRBR Award honors members of the [[Society for Research on Biological Rhythms]] for their contributions.

== Scientific contributions ==
Honma has authored over 200 scholarly articles and has published several edited volumes in the field of chronobiology.<ref>{{Cite web|title=生体リズムの研究|url=https://aschoff-honma.wixsite.com/ahmf/publications|access-date=2021-05-05|website=ahmf|language=ja}}</ref>

Initially, his research revolved around understanding the photic and non-photic entrainment of circadian rhythms and raised hypotheses about the role of feeding in the entrainment of the circadian clock,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Honma K, von Goetz C, Aschoff J | title = Effects of restricted daily feeding on freerunning circadian rhythms in rats | journal = Physiology & Behavior | volume = 30 | issue = 6 | pages = 905–13 | date = June 1983 | pmid = 6611695 | doi = 10.1016/0031-9384(83)90256-1 | s2cid = 20020358 }}</ref> as well as the ways in which endogenous rhythms can entrain to artificial bright light<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Honma K, Honma S, Wada T | title = Entrainment of human circadian rhythms by artificial bright light cycles | journal = Experientia | volume = 43 | issue = 5 | pages = 572–4 | date = May 1987 | pmid = 3582576 | doi = 10.1007/BF02143589 | s2cid = 40116177 }}</ref> before later focusing on uncovering the structure of the circadian clock. Earlier in his career, Honma made the discovery that body temperature, locomotor activity, and plasma levels of [[corticosterone]]—all circadian processes—are likely coupled to one common internal oscillator in rats.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Honma KI, Hiroshige T | title = Internal synchronization among several circadian rhythms in rats under constant light | journal = The American Journal of Physiology | volume = 235 | issue = 5 | pages = R243-9 | date = November 1978 | pmid = 727286 | doi = 10.1152/ajpregu.1978.235.5.R243 }}</ref> However, his current research is centered around the [[ontogeny]] of circadian rhythms<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hiroshige T, Honma K, Watanabe K | title = Ontogeny of the circadian rhythm of plasma corticosterone in blind infantile rats | journal = The Journal of Physiology | volume = 325 | pages = 493–506 | date = April 1982 | pmid = 7108784 | pmc = 1251408 | doi = 10.1113/jphysiol.1982.sp014164 }}</ref> and understanding the [[Physiology|physiological]] aspects of chronobiology. 

=== Earlier works ===
Honma described "a [[phase response curve]] (PRC) to a single bright light pulse in human subjects living under isolation."<ref name=":0">{{cite web | title = Ken-ichi Honma | work = Intercontinental Academia - Nagoya. | url = http://intercontinental-academia.ubias.net/nagoya/people/ken-ichi-honma#:~:text=He%20explored%20the%20human%20circadian,with%20a%20day%2Dnight%20environment }}</ref> He developed a model in animals for a sleep-wake cycle that is desynchronized from other circadian rhythms in the body such as the [[Melatonin|plasma levels of melatonin]].<ref name=":0" />

Honma and his wife, Sato Honma, were able to detect circadian rhythms in [[ARNTL|Bmal1]] gene expression via [[in situ hybridization]] in the SCN of rats. They found that BMAL1 expression was highest during the subjective night in rats and that rhythms of mRNA expression were found in other regions of the brain, like the [[hippocampus]] and the [[cerebellum]].<ref name="pmid9735336">{{cite journal | vauthors = Honma S, Ikeda M, Abe H, Tanahashi Y, Namihira M, Honma K, Nomura M | title = Circadian oscillation of BMAL1, a partner of a mammalian clock gene Clock, in rat suprachiasmatic nucleus | journal = Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications | volume = 250 | issue = 1 | pages = 83–7 | date = September 1998 | pmid = 9735336 | doi = 10.1006/bbrc.1998.9275 }}</ref>

=== Later works ===
In 2014, Honma and his colleagues published a paper that highlighted the effects of postnatal light on [[cryptochrome]]-deficient mice.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|date=2014-01-14|title=Postnatal light overcomes genetic disturbance of circadian rhythms|url=https://www.global.hokudai.ac.jp/blog/postnatal-light-overcomes-genetic-disturbance-of-circadian-rhythms/|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Hokkaido University|language=en}}</ref> The authors showed that exposure to constant light by placing newborn mice in constant light for three weeks after they were born can partially restore rhythms in the SCN, even though the mice lose sleep-wake rhythms upon [[weaning]].<ref name=":2" />

In 2016, he published an article that emphasized the role of physical activity, specifically in blind and elderly people, in the entrainment of circadian rhythms.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal| vauthors = Yamanaka Y, Honma KI, Hashimoto S, Takasu N, Miyazaki T, Honma S |date=2006-10-01|title=Effects of physical exercise on human circadian rhythms |journal=Sleep and Biological Rhythms|language=en|volume=4|issue=3|pages=199–206|doi=10.1111/j.1479-8425.2006.00234.x|issn=1479-8425|hdl=2115/45263|s2cid=73354269 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> The authors demonstrated that physical activity could also shift the plasma levels of melatonin.<ref name=":3" />

In 2017, Ken-Ichi and Sato Honma were part of the team at Hokkaido University that discovered that voltage rhythms in the SCN were synchronized, a finding that became the basis for the theory that the SCN utilizes these synchronized rhythms in order to maintain tissue-wide rhythm.<ref>Hokkaido University. (2017, April 24). {{cite web | title = Synchronized voltage rhythms could maintain the body's clock. | work = ScienceDaily | access-date = April 17, 2021 | url = https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/04/170424093944.htm }}</ref>

In 2019, Honma, with his collaborators, uncovered the role of [[GABAergic|GABAergic neurons]] in inhibiting cells in the [[suprachiasmatic nucleus]] (the central oscillator in mammals). They concluded that [[Gamma-Aminobutyric acid|GABA]] neither establishes nor maintains circadian patterns in the body, but rather that it "refine[s] the circadian firing rhythm to ensure noiseless communications with neurons outside the SCN."<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Mandal DA | date = 9 September 2019 | title = GABA neurons affect the circadian clock. | work = News Medical | url = https://www.news-medical.net/news/20190909/GABA-neurons-affect-the-circadian-clock.aspx }}</ref>

Honma has also been involved with recent research about [[ultradian rhythm]]s, which are short-term rhythms with short-lasting periods.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal | vauthors = Goh GH, Maloney SK, Mark PJ, Blache D | title = Episodic Ultradian Events-Ultradian Rhythms | journal = Biology | volume = 8 | issue = 1 | pages = 15 | date = March 2019 | pmid = 30875767 | doi = 10.3390/biology8010015| pmc=6466064 | doi-access = free }}</ref> He has shown that in constant dark conditions, ultradian rhythms can be observed in the SCN, and that the expression of [[PER1|Per1]], [[PER2|Per2]] and Bmal1—which are central clock genes in mammals—shows ultradian fluctuations and periods of approximately 3 hours.<ref name=":1" /> The research team also showed that these rhythms are most likely [[endogenous]], or that they do not rely on [[Zeitgeber|external cues]] to be generated. Overall, the team concluded that ultradian rhythms had no correlation with the animal's physical activity rhythms, but further research is still needed.<ref name=":1" />

Honma was a prominent anti-[[Japan Standard Time|daylight savings]] movement-person in Japan, advocating against the establishment of daylight-savings time in Japan by educating people on the detrimental health effects associated with the misalignment of the body's clock and the light-dark cycles ([[zeitgeber]]s). Currently, Japan does not have any [[daylight saving time]] system in place.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Roenneberg T, Winnebeck EC, Klerman EB | title = Daylight Saving Time and Artificial Time Zones - A Battle Between Biological and Social Times | journal = Frontiers in Physiology | volume = 10 | pages = 944 | date = August 7, 2019 | pmid = 31447685 | doi = 10.3389/fphys.2019.00944 | pmc = 6692659 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
